The pitch was reliable and well-rehearsed. A well-spoken young man would call you on the telephone — perhaps you were a retired accountant in Aarau, or a plumber from Zug who had built a business from scratch over thirty years. He would tell you about Balluun, a Swiss technology company based in Zürich, backed by prominent names from the world of Swiss finance. He would mention a planned listing on the SIX Swiss Exchange, then the Nasdaq. He might drop the name of former Julius Bär CEO Walter Knabenhans, or IT entrepreneur Ariel Lüdi. He would tell you the shares were going for CHF 6.50, but that number would be CHF 10.50 by the following year and CHF 26.40 by 2022. He would create a deadline. He would call back.

Behind many of those calls was a company called Savendis AG, registered in Glattbrugg and later Zürich, with a president named Thomas André Hippin, born 10 September 1985, citizen of Zürich. And behind Savendis was a structure designed — whether intentionally or consequentially — to ensure that the maximum amount of money stuck to the brokers and the minimum amount reached the company whose shares were being sold.

The Machinery

Savendis AG was incorporated in December 2011. Its stated purpose was to broker and market companies and company shares — a broadly worded mandate that covered, in practice, the telephone sale of pre-IPO startup equity to private investors with no experience in venture capital and no means of independently verifying the claims being made to them.

Thomas Hippin was the sole board member and president throughout the companys existence. He operated from an address on Stockerstrasse in central Zürich — a respectable street, a plausible letterhead.

"Go to Zürich. The young men driving Ferraris around the city — those are the brokers."

— A Balluun investor, quoted in the NZZ, 2021

The most documented case involves Balluun AG, a B2B e-commerce startup founded in 2009 by two German brothers who had since exited. Balluun had assembled a credibility-lending board featuring the former Bank Julius Bär CEO Walter Knabenhans and Ariel Lüdi, who had famously sold the e-commerce firm Hybris to SAP for CHF 1.5 billion. The presence of such names was the architecture of trust upon which the whole telephone operation rested.

Savendis was one of several Zürich-based brokerage firms — alongside Norcore, Finoris, Vimes, and Centurium — selling Balluun shares by phone. The NZZ, which investigated the Balluun affair in multiple reports between 2018 and 2021, obtained purchase documents from a Balluun shareholder who had dealt with Savendis. What those documents revealed was instructive: the selling entity was not Savendis AG directly but a Malta-registered company. Payment went to a bank account in Liechtenstein, not Switzerland. Share prices ranged from CHF 0.50 to CHF 13.00 per share depending on the broker. Broker commissions ran up to 50% of the purchase price. Of approximately CHF 55 million raised by all brokers combined, only CHF 24 million reached Balluun AG — per Balluun managements own admission. The gap of roughly CHF 31 million was retained by the brokers.

When the NZZ put specific questions to Thomas Hippin about the Savendis operation, he confirmed that the firm had raised capital for Balluun during a period of liquidity difficulties. He insisted that the Balluun management had been aware of the share sales. As to how much commission Savendis had taken: he declined to say.

The Investors

The NZZs reporting on the Balluun affair established a clear profile of who the brokers were calling — and why the calls worked. The target lists were segmented. Some call sheets, reported the NZZ, contained populations where seventy percent of the names were people aged 75 or older. The ideal target was a successful tradesperson or professional — someone who had built genuine wealth through hard work but had limited experience of financial markets and no particular reason to doubt a caller who sounded knowledgeable and cited prominent Swiss businessmen.

The mechanics of the sale exploited a structural vulnerability in Swiss financial law. Telephone brokers selling unlisted shares were, under the relevant conditions, not required to hold a FINMA licence. The FINMA itself acknowledged to the NZZ that it lacked the legal basis to maintain a general named warning list covering such firms and individuals. This created a grey zone that operations like Savendis could exploit with relative impunity for years.

"After buying shares once via a telephone salesman, I am now regularly contacted by various brokers. I am sitting on many illiquid holdings and want to sell them."

— A Balluun shareholder, NZZ, 2021

The investor, once contacted and once having purchased, entered a kind of secondary market of vulnerability. Their contact details were traded between brokerage firms — the NZZ reported that investor lists were actively sold among the operators on the Zürich market. Those who had lost money were, paradoxically, the most susceptible to subsequent approaches: a new caller would suggest that the loss could be recovered by investing at the current, lower price to reduce the average cost. Many investors did so. Many invested a second time. And a third.

The Collapse

Balluun AG never listed on any exchange. The promised SIX Swiss Exchange IPO, originally projected for Q4 2016, never happened. The planned Nasdaq listing did not happen. The companys core software — a B2B trade fair platform intended to create a virtual exhibition experience — failed to gain commercial traction. In 2018, Balluun acquired a British software company called Saigara in an attempt to pivot to B2C. That acquisition failed to rescue the business.

In December 2020, the Konkursrichterin of the Bezirksgericht Zürich declared Balluun AG bankrupt. The company was dissolved. Its roughly 1,000 shareholders — many of whom had paid between CHF 6.50 and CHF 13 per share on the basis of telephone recommendations — lost their entire investment. The bankruptcy proceedings were formally closed on 10 January 2025.

A lawyer representing affected investors filed a criminal complaint against a firm and its employees with the competent public prosecutor in December 2020. The complaint named specific conduct, specific individuals. Whether this led to formal criminal proceedings against Hippin specifically is not confirmed in publicly available court records at time of publication.

Savendis AG entered liquidation in June 2020 — the same month FINMA was watching. It was struck from the commercial register in December 2020, the month Balluun went bankrupt.

The Attic Flat in Altendorf

While his investors were losing their savings, Thomas Hippin had been living in a 4½-room attic flat at Maienwies 9 in Altendorf, Kanton Schwyz — a premium address in a gated residential complex with a large garden, assessed by the cantonal authorities at CHF 1,300,000.

The forced auction of a CHF 1.3 million attic apartment by the cantonal enforcement office is the public record of a man whose liabilities had overtaken his assets. Whether those liabilities arose directly from investor claims, unpaid creditors of Savendis, or personal financial mismanagement is not established in the available public record. What is established is the sequence: company liquidated, criminal complaint filed, apartment seized and auctioned — all within the same twelve-month window.

The Black Sea

By 2021, Thomas Hippin had relocated to Burgas, Bulgaria — a city on the Black Sea coast, the fourth-largest in the country, and one that offers EU residency, low living costs, and a three-hour flight from Zürich. He had reinvented himself as the Resort Manager of Residenz Victoria, a luxury gated development targeting German and Swiss retirees looking to emigrate or purchase second homes on the Black Sea.

The marketing model — Swiss and German phone contacts selling property in a foreign jurisdiction to older buyers — structurally resembles the Savendis model in certain respects. No evidence of specific wrongdoing at Residenz Victoria has been established at time of publication.

The website for Residenz Victoria emphasises the Swiss management pedigree, the stability of the EU jurisdiction, the health benefits of the Black Sea climate, and the investment potential of the properties. The persuasion architecture is familiar: credibility through perceived Swiss-German professionalism, a foreign asset with limited independent verification, a target audience of people who have worked hard and accumulated savings.

What the Pattern Shows

The Savendis operation was not, legally speaking, straightforwardly criminal in its design — the FINMA itself acknowledged the regulatory gap that allowed telephone brokers selling unlisted shares to operate without authorisation. What made Savendis and its peers corrosive was the systematic targeting of vulnerable investors, the opacity of the Malta-Liechtenstein transaction structure, the undisclosed commission levels of up to fifty percent, and the fundamental dishonesty of the sales pitch: these were not safe investments, these were not certain IPOs, and the brokers knew it.

Of the approximately CHF 55 million raised from ordinary Swiss investors for Balluun shares, roughly CHF 31 million — according to Balluuns own management — never reached the company. It went to the brokers. Not all of that is attributable to Savendis alone. But Savendis was named by multiple investors, documented in NZZ purchase records, and confirmed by Hippin himself as a capital-raising intermediary for Balluun.

The investors who bought those shares at CHF 6.50, CHF 10, CHF 13, who were promised a Nasdaq listing by 2018 and a share price of CHF 26.40 by 2022 — they got nothing. Their attic flats were not seized. They did not relocate to the Black Sea.

This article is based exclusively on publicly available information including NZZ reporting \(2018–2021\), the official Betreibungsamt Altendorf-Lachen auction publication \(October 2021\), Northdata company history for Savendis AG \(CHE-205.518.334\), the Residenz Victoria website \(residenz-victoria.ch\), and Moneyhouse records for Balluun AG. Thomas Hippin is presumed innocent in any matter not subject to a final court verdict. No criminal conviction against Hippin is confirmed in publicly available records at time of publication. References to structural similarities between past and present business models are analytical observations, not allegations of current wrongdoing.
